doc.title: Percy Humphrey Band: Percy Humphrey, Jim Robinson, Ernest Roubleau, Josiah Frazier Interview, 1972-02-29

title: Whether early jazz grew from brass band and march music
summary: The interviewer asks how much jazz came from brass band music; a speaker explains the doubled march rhythm and improvisation.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: How much of the old music came from, I think, we were talking to Dick yesterday afternoon, I was thinking that, you know, entrance of the gladiators, that one, it goes into That's A Plenty. Oh, yeah. Right? Well, it's close. It might have some positives. I wonder how much early jazz came out of martial music, brass band music, I mean music that never was written for the 2-4 beat, that was written for the 1-3 beat. I wonder how much early jazz came out of brass band music. You know, brass band music. At one time, from my understanding, at one time, that was practically all you had, brass band music, like the suits and marches and all that stuff. See, that's the reason you hear the phrase about circus music, see? Yeah. Circus will hit a town and to attract attention, they'd take any march. Yeah. We had so many honesty goodness rehearsals, you know, guys would hardly miss a note. Oh, yeah. They'd play it on, what's that, what you call that, that double time, see? Oh, yeah, yeah. They'd play it on that double time. Bop, bop, bop, bop, bop. Yeah. And everybody, they wouldn't miss a step or nothing else. They wouldn't miss a step or nothing else. That drum all he could do, the beat, they'd say boom, the snare drum, say bop, bop, bop. That's right. And they marched and they're just, you know what I mean? Oh, school children, man. I can't do that. Let's go. You think sometimes this military stuff was kind of fast, but those circuses, when they say circus music, that means you're racehorses, see? Yeah, they're going, man. They're going. But now, to get back to what you said, the whole lot of the music we play now, I'd say is derivative from a whole lot of marches is copied right behind them. The only thing is, well, your marches, your rhythm going to say, chink, chink, you see? And they don't go that way. And I said they double it up, see? That's the way they do it now. But like if you, the brass band stuff, that bass drum hit one that snap drum answer. Anson, yeah. See? Your bass horn say, whoop, the mellophones and whatnot, they make the answer. Yeah. See? But now, instead of one doing just one section on the, on the, on the, on the, what, the phrase or whatever you call it, they're doubling up all the way on it. See? They're single for a while. Yeah. See? But they give it the pep and the shove that, what we consider in jazz, see? They improvise on it, see? They add to it, to it, what, the original score, see? And they play it the way they feel it should be played. Forget about the music and the way the, the brass bands been playing it. See? That is that particular type brass band. Yeah, yeah. See? The military bands and the school bands and whatnot. Any of you give much to the theory that jazz came out of spirituals? Does this, you know, does this hold much more? Yeah.
